sentences.text: This animal was a tiny hunter roughly one and a half meters in length with a mass near five kilograms, though other estimates suggest a height of thirty centimeters and a weight of two kilograms.
Its anatomy combined features seen in dromaeosaurids, troodontids, and early bird-like creatures, including hollow bones and feathers.
The teeth possessed exceptionally long roots that accounted for approximately seventy percent of the total tooth length.
The genus name honors black-hatted performers in Buddhist Cham dance, while the species name references the former rock layer name.
Sharp claws on the middle toe were likely adapted to climb over the backs of larger animals.
Alan Turner, Sunny Hai-Ching Hwang, and Mark Norell formally named and described the species in 2007.
Evidence of rapid movement and high activity levels suggests the creature maintained a warm body temperature.
It probably moved through the forest canopy by gliding between trees using its four limbs as wings.
Although often placed within dromaeosaurids, some scientists doubt this placement, and the Paleobiology Database lists its parent group as Microraptorinae.
Fossils date from the Berriasian to the Albian stages, spanning between 143.1 and 100.5 million years ago.
A 2012 analysis positioned Shanag as a sister taxon to the Unenlagiinae, but a 2017 study recovered it as a dromaeosaurid sister to Late Cretaceous Laurasian forms, excluding a link to Unenlagiinae.
